HEAD OFFICE: 21 Front St. East, Toronto 


Fish Grow On Trees 


Our publicly owned forests supply industry, 
nourish wildlife and store the water which 
feeds the thousands of streams where fight¬ 
ing fish abound. One third of our primary 
production and all our outdoor vacations 
depend on forest trees. 

Last year, 86 per cent of forest fires were 
caused by human carelessness. 

This year, be positive your camp fire is out 
before you leave it. Be scrupulously careful 
with smoking materials. Be sure you do not 
cause the tragic waste of forest fire. 

Our Forests Need You 
You Need Our Forests 

HON. J. W. SPOONER, Minister 



ONTARIO 



F. A. MacDOUGALL, Deputy Minister 


ONTARIO DEPARTMENT OF LANDS AND FORESTS

Canadian Camping 




A 

FOURTH 

TERM 


EDITORIAL 


R. H. Perry 
Director, Camp Kawabi 


Back in 1929 the Camping twins, 
Messrs. Dimock and Hendry, authors 
of “Camping and Character” stated 
that one of the major current tenden¬ 
cies of camping is the shift from a rec¬ 
reational to an educational function. 

This statement was made nearly thirty 
years ago so it would be reasonable to 
assume that the shift has taken place 
and that Camping is now a wholly ed¬ 
ucational activity. But is this so? How 
many Summer Camps regard them¬ 
selves as educational units, or consider 
that they are engaged in an education¬ 
al activity? 

I think everyone would agree that 
there is a difference between Schooling 
and Camping and that while Camping 
may be an “educational function”, the 
two activities have little in common, 
except that both are concerned with 
the growth and development of chil¬ 
dren. 

Education is largely a matter of 
academics, with books, mental exercises 
and examinations. Camping has to do 
with living out of doors and the ac¬ 
tivities associated with this type of life. 
There is quite a difference between 
teaching a boy to swim and teaching 


him Latin. The one is physical, the 
other mental. Schooling takes place in¬ 
doors and it is, or should be, hard 
work. It is not always a joyful experi¬ 
ence for the youngster and he has little 
choice in what he does, and further¬ 
more, he has to stay at it. 

Camping on the other hand is fun 
and everything is made attractive. The 
school principal gets his pupils whether 
he wants them or not, but the Camp 
Director goes all out to fill his Camp, 
assuring everyone that there is nothing 
quite so wonderful as his Camp X. 
School is routine and the word “dis¬ 
cipline” keeps popping up. Camp pro¬ 
vides variety, and control is hidden by 
the magic words “positive suggestion”. 

The point we are trying to make 
is that School and Camp are different, 
but this does not mean Camping is less 
important. If we could accept this, 
Summer Camping might attain the 
status of a Fourth Term in the year’s 
development of the child. 

As persons interested in Camping 
and Children, our approach to the 
needs of Campers and their develop¬ 
ment might be more dedicated if we 
would accept the Fourth Term idea 
and work toward better staff, better 
training and greater usefulness. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, April 1959 


115 



A NOTE ABOUT . . . 


THE SHORTER 
GAMP TERM 

This is a brief appraisal of a situation 
for which wc are not responsible and 
which was first viewed with disap¬ 
proval. 

Twenty-five to thirty years ago, at 
least 80% of the campers attending our 
boys’ private camps, were enrolled for 
the full eight-week term. We believed 
that this was the desirable period for 
a boy to attend camp, and did every¬ 
thing we could to encourage the prac¬ 
tice. However, over the years a definite 
change has taken place. It is now the 
exception rather than the rule for 
campers to spend the full eight weeks 
at camp. A half season, or four weeks, 
has become accepted as the normal 
camping period. 

Why has this change taken place? 
We are not sure that we know, but it 
is probable that the answer is not a 
simple one. If parents were asked, we 
know many would say that they want 
their sons to have camping experience 
at an organized camp, but they also 
want them to spend some part of the 
summer vacation with the family, and 
especially during the father’s vacation, 
so that the whole family may be to¬ 
gether. 

With this practice we find ourselves 
in complete agreement and cannot 
honestly argue against it, even though 
it presents us with a difficult problem. 
For boys to spend approximately half 
of their summer vacation at camp and 
the remainder with their families, we 
believe is in their best interests and 
it is a situation we must accept. 

What, then, are some of the effects 
of this changed situation to which we 


F, M. Van Wagner , Director, 
Camp Nominingue, Labelle Co., Quebec . 


are referring? The first problem with 
which we are faced is that more parents 
wish their sons to attend camp for the 
first, rather than the second half period. 
The resulting imbalance between the 
first and second half enrolment is, for 
very obvious reasons, not a happy situ¬ 
ation for any camp. i 

We believe that as far as a boy’s 
camping experience is concerned, there 
is no choice between the two periods. 
This statement has been made to 
parents repeatedly, with little effect. 
More applications are still received for 
the first half than for the second half, 
and we know of nothing we can do to 
change this uneconomic situation. For¬ 
tunately, there are usually a few coun¬ 
sellors who wish to spend only the first 
half season at camp, and commonly a 
few more, when their examination re¬ 
sults are known, wish to leave before 
the end of the season. This helps a 
little, budget wise. 

In past years we found that, while 
many boys enjoyed the full eight weeks 
at camp, there were others who tired 
of camp before the end of the season. 
We now believe that one of the most 
desirable results of the shorter period 
at camp is that camp life never be¬ 
comes monotonous, and campers are 
not looking forward to leaving before 
the end of their scheduled stay. No 
more do we find a need for special 
events to promote enthusiasm, raise 
morale and off-set the effects of mon¬ 
otony. We now realize that one of the 
most favourable outcomes of this 
changed situation is a more relaxed, 
enthusiastic and happy camp through¬ 
out the season. 

We know that some other private 
camps have to cope with a similar sit¬ 
uation. It would be interesting to know 
their reactions to it. —* 


116 


Canadian Camping 


D . E. Allan, Director, 1955, 
Camp Manitou for Boys, 
Winnipeg, Manitoba 


Twenty-nine years ago, the Rotary 
Club of Winnipeg, due to depression 
circumstances in the city, decided to 
offer a camping experience for needy 
boys. 

A camp site was located approxi¬ 
mately fifteen miles from Winnipeg 
during a winter outing snow-shoe trip. 
Arrangements were made through the 
Winnipeg Foundation to secure the 
land on the Assiniboine River in order 
to establish the first camp site. 

In 1931, the first camping venture 
was held, with twenty boys attending 
for a two-week period. The cost per 
boy averaged $5.00 which was met by 
the Service Club. Facilities at that time 
consisted of a marquee tent serving as 
kitchen and dining area; the boys slept 
in tents. 

The following year brought greater 
interest in the project, and the Win¬ 
nipeg Y.M.C.A. was asked to share in 
the operation by providing the leader¬ 
ship and direction of the venture. 
Manitou continued to expand and de¬ 
velop, both in terms of its following, 
purpose and philosophy. Facilities, by 
this time, had outgrown tents, and 
boys were now housed in boxcars do¬ 
nated by the railways, and converted 
into cabins. More ground had been 
cleared, and a well bored to replace the 
cumbersome method of transporting 
water by tank truck. By 1939, seven 
major Service Clubs in Winnipeg were 
involved in the Manitou operation; 
boys from all parts of the city were 
attending over a now-expanded period 
of six weeks. Subsidy per boy was now 
about 50% of the camper cost, in 
order that the boys from needy families 
could attend, with many boys being 
completely subsidized. 


WE HAVE 
A UNIQUE 
CAMP 

On application by letters patent in 
1939, Manitou became an incorporated 
company with the shares being held 
by the seven service clubs. As the need 
for low-cost camping on a high level 
increased, the site was developed from 
its meagre start of tents and boxcars 
to the present thirty-four acres which 
includes three large playing fields, 
twenty-three permanent buildings for 
campers and staff, and a large dining 
hall and kitchen. 

Although the cost of camping has 
increased manyfold, the purpose and 
philosophy of the Manitou directorate 
has not varied from its original start. 
The present operational budget has in¬ 
creased from several hundred dollars in 
the beginning to presently $13,000 an¬ 
nually with one third of this derived 
from fees and income; the balance de¬ 
rived from the shareholders. 

The Assiniboine River proved un¬ 
suitable four years ago for swimming, 
so plans were made to construct a 
swimming pool to meet the need. Once 
again the shareholders rose to the oc¬ 
casion, and donated the necessary funds 
over and above the regular grants, to 
build the 88,000 gallon swimming pool. 

The camp derives its campers from 
Red Feather agencies in the Greater 
Winnipeg Area, Juvenile and Family 
Court, Children’s Aid Society, Family 
Bureau, Y.M.C.A., Neighbourhood and 
Settlement Houses, Child Guidance 
Centres, and so on. These boys are re- 

continued on page 158 


Toronto , Canada , April 1959

THE SEARCH FOR LEADERS 

Martin Gold 

Research Center for Group Dynamics } University of Michigan 
New Jersey Federation of YM-YWHA’s Camps 


Here follows the address of Mr. Gold as it was presented at the 
Annual Banquet of the Ontario Camping Association Conference , King 
Edward Hotel , Toronto , on Saturday , March 7, 1959. 


Leaders are the dynamic of a camp. 
They are the motors which set a camp 
humming. With leadership, the most 
poorly-equipped camp is a treasure- 
house of things to do; without leader¬ 
ship, the best-equipped camp can be 
deadly as a child’s rainy Sunday. No 
wonder camp directors invest so much 
time, money, energy, and concern in 
their search for leaders. Fortunately, 
leadership is a central issue for others 
than campers who thereby gain some 
helpful partners in their search. 

These partners to whom I refer are 
social scientists—mainly social psychol¬ 
ogists — whose literature includes a 
mass of more or less rigorous investiga¬ 
tions of leadership in an effort to 
understand it. Hardly a text is pub¬ 
lished in the field without a chapter on 
“Leadership”, or “Social Power”, or 
“Elites”, or “Social Ascendancy”, or 
under some other label by which the 
phenomenon is known. One such chap¬ 
ter cites no less than one hundred and 
eleven other separate references. I cer¬ 
tainly will not attempt to review this 
literature here. But I will try to bring 
the major outlines of this research to 
terms with the problem of campmen’s 
search for leaders. 

For if I have anything to offer to 
campmen on this subject, it is because 


I am a campman and a social psychol¬ 
ogist as well. I have found a happy 
coincidence in my two jobs, researching 
for nine months, camping for three. 
There is a great deal of research in 
human relations, accomplished and in 
progress, which is relevant to organized 
camping. A significant proportion of it 
has actually been done in camp set¬ 
tings: research on cabin groups working 
together, on attitude change at camp, 
and on the establishment of leadership, 
to name a few problems. I have found 
much of it directly relevant to camp 
organization and programming. Some 
of my own research got its original 
impetus from problems I encountered 
at camp. 

One of the first things to strike a 
reader in the scientific literature on 
leadership, after its tremendous volume, 
is the fact that the word “leader” 
applies to a lot of different types of 
individuals. I think the same thing is 
true, and perhaps more so, when camp- 
men discuss leaders. We’re not really 
agreed on what a leader is and this 
makes it difficult for us to search for 
leaders together. We’re not sure what 
we’re looking for, and it is sometimes 
doubtful whether we will know a leader 
when we see one. We are in much the 
same predicament as Milne’s Winnie- 
the-Pooh and Piglet looking for the 


118 


Canadian Camping 


Hefalump, neither having the vaguest 
notion of what a Hefalump looked like. 
This image of Pooh and Piglet tramp¬ 
ing through the Deep Woods after 
Hefalump is especially appropriate in 
connection with our own search for 
leaders. Because, some of you will re¬ 
member, Pooh and Piglet eventually 
realized they were following their own 
tracks; in effect, looking for themselves. 

Suppose we call up our personal 
images of “the leader”, placing him in 
his characteristic pose and his natural 
setting. What does he look like? 

Does he assume a tall, heroic stance 
on the lake shore, his campers ranged 
about him gaped-mouthed as he points 
to a flight of geese winging into the 
sun? Do we see a pretty young lady in 
the glow of firelight, spinning a magic 
story for her girls? Or is our “leader” 
an energetic young man in the third 
base coaching box, masterminding a 
squeeze bunt for his boys? Is he a skill¬ 
ed discussion leader who, by his inti¬ 
mate grasp of his group’s dynamics, 
knows just when to speak and when to 
keep silent, so they will decide what he 
has already in mind? Or is our image 
one of a counsellor with an arm about 
the shoulders of one happy child? 

These are all appropriate leader 
images. A social scientist ideally de¬ 
fines which one he has in mind and 
goes on researching from there. But 
selecting an image is a somewhat dif¬ 
ferent process for campmen. For any 
one’s own ideal is not a matter for 
arbitrary definition but depends on 
the kind of camp he wants to run. 
Ultimately, his definition of “leader” is 
a function of his values and the motiv¬ 
ations which brought him into camping. 
When we face the issue squarely, the 
“leader” is a projection of our values, 
an image we create ourselves and 
forthwith go in search of it. 


Which brings me to a theme I sound 
again and again. In our search for 
leaders, as in every other aspect of 
camp organization, our first step is 
always to clarify our value positions. 
What are we trying to do for campers 
at camp? What are our criteria for a 
“successful season?” What do we con¬ 
sider a “good camper?” All of these 
questions are related to the problem of 
camp leadership. If we are able to 
answer them, we clarify our values and, 
in so doing, describe the leader we 
want at camp. 

Some people approach this value 
issue as a completely individual affair. 
“You have your values, I have mine.” 
I find it hard to argue against this 
approach since I have some knowledge 
of widely divergent cultures with such 
disparate values, it is hard to reconcile 
them. But this individual relativity 
view of values makes me terribly un¬ 
comfortable, especially when I’m think¬ 
ing about camping. It seems to me all 
our camps share certain goals, and the 
attempt to reach these goals generates 
certain common values which are rele¬ 
vant to camp programme. 

There are essentially two main goals 
in our camping as I see it. One is to 
help children have fun. Now, fun means 
in part the high spots of a season, like 
special treats and trips and events. It 
also means the wild times, when 
campers giggle so hysterically they 
can’t stop themselves. But these make 
icing for a more substantial cake. Fun 
for a boy or girl, in the sense of the 
deep satisfaction which makes camp a 
wonderful place, a place to go back to 
summer after summer, involves a par¬ 
ticular and significant experience. It is 
an experience in which a child discovers 
himself as a worthwhile, a respectable 
individual. He learns he can cope with 
the world successfully and, beyond even 
that, that he can create in it. 


Toronto, Canada , April 1959 


119 



This self-actualization notion as the 
essential joy in camping suggests spe¬ 
cific standards for camp programme 
and leadership. It suggests, for example, 
that programme includes a place for 
every constructive talent, and that no 
one skill, be it baseball or basketweav¬ 
ing, is so emphasized and honored as 
to create categories of elites and inepts 
among campers. The image of a leader 
is created which includes an element 
of curiosity about a wide variety of 
things and an appreciation for all sorts 
of efforts. This leader can teach what 
he knows, and it is hoped he knows a 
lot; but, equally important, he wants 
to learn what he doesn’t know and 
isn’t ashamed of learning along with or 
from a child. And this leader maintains 
behavior standards among campers by 
means other than force of will, author¬ 
ity, or degradation. 

The second goal of camping fits com¬ 
fortably with the first. It recognizes the 
obligation a camp owes to the society 
in which it flourishes and the unique 
service it can perform for its commun¬ 
ity. It seems to me a camp should aim 
to help its campers become better 
citizens for a democracy. It should 
provide experiences in which children 
can weigh alternatives and make de¬ 
cisions, can find themselves in major¬ 
ities and minorities, can speak and 
listen, and can discover that the other 
fellow is just as sure he’s right. Camp 
is a unique setting in which to provide 
children with these experiences. For 
nowhere else is the setting so dedicated 
to children’s interests. Camp is the 
children’s world. Decisions are often 
cut down to their size: whether to hike 
or play ball, who gets the tennis courts 
on Tuesday afternoons, what can be 
done to make a stay in the infirmary 
less boring. 

Camp misses its exceptional oppor¬ 
tunity to develop democratic citizen¬ 


ship if it does not key its programme 
for it. This means campers must be en¬ 
couraged to participate in programme 
planning and be given a hand in camp 
government to the edge of limits set by 
adult responsibility. These considera¬ 
tions contribute further to the leader 
image. The ideal becomes a person who 
need not control situations, but can 
allow his campers some rein. He is able 
to point out realities in order to help 
his campers make sound plans, but he 
lets them make mistakes they can learn 
from, too. Democracy for him is not 
letting campers have his way but help¬ 
ing them decide their own. 

I’ve sketched a value position which 
leads to a particular description of a 
leader. But there is an important ele¬ 
ment of leadership unaccounted for 
still, which is that a person is not a 
leader unless someone follows him. That 
is, whatever values a counsellor might 
represent, we would not consider him 
a leader if he did not command the 
respect of his campers and if he was 
not able to influence them. We cannot 
assume that, because a counsellor rep¬ 
resents our image of a leader, he rep¬ 
resents the campers’ images, too. It 
may be that our values are not shared 
by the children at all, and that our 
ideal would not become their leader. 
For, after all, we can, by making a 
someone a counsellor, only nominate 
him for leader; in a very real sense, 
the campers must elect him. C. A. Gibb 
of the University of Melbourne, and an 
expert on leadership research, makes 
an important distinction between head¬ 
ship and leadership: headship is the 
position of a person who gets his 
authority from outisde the group he 
heads; leadership is granted only by 
the group itself. A director appoints a 
counsellor to leadership; the campers 
will or will not make him leader. 

continued on page 135

THE MEANING OF HANDCRAFT 


Anne Parke 


I have been given the delightful 
opportunity of writing an article on 
what the word HANDCRAFT means 
to me as a layman. With much humil¬ 
ity I shall attempt to transfer my en¬ 
thusiasm, to you! 

Before we go any further, I feel I 
must explain, my training in handcraft 
is nil, but my experience is varied. 
Actually one doesn’t need professional 
training in this line to be able to 
successfully entice your young campers’ 
interest. 

Begin with reverting your thoughts 
to when you were a child! Your 
imagination was a free agent. Anything 
you didn’t have in your indian games 
or cowboy games, you improvised with 
blankets, string etc. Children today we 
say have so many advantages over us.... 
Yes, they have more modern schools, 
parks, and homes fully equipped with 
beautiful living rooms for the adults 
and a large tidy playroom for the 
youngsters. But banish the soul who 
dares to leave a mess behind, or even 
begin to create one. The playroom must 
stay the way it originally was pictured 
when Mom and Dad first saw it in the 
Better Homes Magazine. 

Now, at camp you have these chil¬ 
dren away from home, with every pos¬ 
sible opportunity about you. This is 
where you can find the meaning of 
HANDCRAFT. No shiny floors to keep 
shiny, and all sorts of material at your 
finger tips. Here you can reach the 


natural creative instinct in these chil¬ 
dren. Every one of them has it if you 
work hard enough to find it. I repeat 
bring yourself to their level of thinking. 

Handcraft has always been to me 
“something you make from nothing”; 
in other words something you create 
from a “nothing”, or to be more ex¬ 
plicit, from Waste Products. My re¬ 
sources, moneywisc, with any group I 
have ever worked, has been very low. 
This in itself presented the first chal¬ 
lenge. How to keep forty to fifty chil¬ 
dren busy approximately one hour each 
day, ten days at a stretch and little or 
no funds with which to operate? 

Begin with the age groups . .. How 
many? .. . How many daily one-hour 
sessions will you be required to have, 
so that your sessions don’t lag (waiting 
for the younger child to catch up with 
the older one). Plan what you are going 
to accomplish each day; don’t make it 
too much; then you won’t be leaving 
projects unfinished at the end of camp. 
But in the event that you have a more 
speedy youngster in the group, have a 
list of preparations to be made for the 
next session, that he can do, or even 
have a simple little project that can 
be picked up at random. But in any 
event do not let this child advance 
ahead of the group, otherwise you will 
have repercussions on both sides. Be 
prepared for him, for there is one or 
more in every group! 

Don’t give the children something to 
do that they have done all winter long 


Toronto , Canada , April 1959 


121 



in school or church groups — such as 
sewing stuffed toys, etc. To elaborate 
more fully: my pet camp project, or 
material, is papier mache. It can be 
used in the following articles, and this 
is only a small part of the list: 

Beads—jewellery—Indian Masks — 
Vases — Animals and puppets. 

There isn't a child I have met who 
didn’t enjoy working with papier 
mache or clay and with their camping 
clothes on and no one to tell them to 
watch the floor. What better oppor¬ 
tunity! Get into it up to your elbows 
if you like! 

From the above suggestions choose 
a main project for eveyone — Indian 
Masks will be finished and painted by 
the time you have Indian Day at camp 
(prearranged), they can all be on dis¬ 
play). A one-hour session in one day 
is required to prepare paper and flour 
and also draw the sketch of what de¬ 
sign you are going to make. Always 
have one sample of every project, that 
you yourself have made. Therefore 
you know what can be done, and any 
difficulties that will arise beforehand. 

Having made a sample, you will 
know approximately how many hours 
or days it will take for it to dry. Now, 
then, if you have several short projects 
such as beads, puppets, decorating bal¬ 
loons, to fill in, when the time comes 
to paint your major projects — masks 
or puppets, vases etc. — then they will 
be attacked with real anticipation and 
zeal. 

Ideas are limitless but to give you a 
few more to work with: 

INDIAN TOM TOM — for Indian 
Day; made from Ice Cream Cartons, 
painted with Indian designs. 

INDIAN HEADPIECES — corru¬ 
gated cardboard cut in V/i" strips; 


smooth side can be decorated with 
crayons, and the holes will hold feathers 
found around camp, or previously do¬ 
nated from a nearby farmer. If these 
cannot be found, then use construction 
paper and make your own feathers. 

Bedding Companies receive much of 
their goods sewn up in potato sacking. 
With a little imagination these can be 
transformed into Tee Pees sewn with 
string and large eye’d needles. Indian 
Signs can be painted on. 

Perhaps the camp leaders would like 
to have a play.... you’d be surprised 
what effects can be produced for 
scenery by using large cardboard car¬ 
tons (lots of these at a camp) and 
tempra paints. 

For another fill-in suggestion, weav¬ 
ing can he done quite cheaply using 
crepe paper. With empty spools, cut 
your crepe paper as it comes in the 
package to /a" wide; twist the end 
piece and thread through hole in spool, 
pull through, continue until all the 
paper is through, this gives the crepe 
paper the affect of Raffia at a fraction 
of the cost of the real Raffia. Cut circles 
of cardboard and use these for weaving 
cards. Bobby pins can be used instead 
of needles. 

Branches of trees (dead ones) can 
be used in scenery, and blossoms can 
be added with crepe paper, hairpins or 
light weight wire. 

Vases can be made with old pickle 
jars, covered with papier mache. Paint 
on design when dry. 

Balloons.make carboard feet; 

construction paper cut-out for ears, 
eyes, hair, nose, etc., stick on with little 
hinges of scotch tape. This of course is 
one idea that presents a fair outlay of 
expense. Try to avoid this! But if you

Canadian Camping 



AN INDIAN GOUNCIL PROGRAMME 


In response to the many requests for Mr . Jack 
Eslaugh's material , we are pleased to reprint 
this article . . . 


On occasion, camping people have 
been heard to remark. “I’d like to have 
an Indian programme but I don’t think 
I could ever get into the part of being 
the chief at a Council Ring.” It is my 
conviction that anyone who can work 
successfully with children, can achieve 
success with an Indian Lore pro¬ 
gramme. It means reaching to the 
child’s level of interest. It requires that 
you dress for the part and it asks that 
you become enchanted. It takes time 
and experience to feel at home in any 
make-believe activity; but the campers 
will be right with anyone who is intent 
on making a success of the Indian Lore 
programme. The presence of spectators 
can be a bit unnerving at first. It is 
much more comfortable when everyone 
at the council ring is an “Indian”. So 
for the first two or three councils that 
you conduct, perhaps you could ar¬ 
range for spectators to be otherwise 
occupied. 

The chief is the central figure in the 
Council Ring ceremony and therefore 
the camp director is often the logical 
person for this role. There is consider¬ 
able prestige in being the Chief, and it 
is sometimes a problem for senior staff 
to feel comfortable under the leader¬ 
ship of someone else. If this problem 
can be resolved, there is no reason at 
all why some other person shouldn’t 
make a specialty of Indian Lore and 


carry the program. However, the choice 
of a leader is important. A poorly or¬ 
ganized or inadequately rehearsed pro¬ 
gramme can be most discouraging. And 
when a programme has failed, it is 
often difficult to arouse interest and 
enthusiasm for another try. 

If the leader is genuinely interested 
in Indian Lore and will take the time 
and trouble to do some research and 
study, the initial programmes should 
be moderately successful. Indian Lore 
is an expanding programme. Given 
good leadership, it can be built up over 
the years until it becomes an establish¬ 
ed tradition in any camp. 

The choice of a site for the Council 
Ring is important. Select an area 
reasonably remote from any buildings, 
and develop a path free from obstruc¬ 
tions, as it will often be quite dark 
when your campers return. A flat space 
some fifty feet in diameter, surrounded 
by trees will lend enchantment. At¬ 
mosphere is very important. Any roots 
or stones should be removed from the 
flat space which is going to be used for 
Indian games and dances. 

The Council Ring and the path 
leading to it lend themselves to de¬ 
velopment. Find another spot for the 
ordinary camp fires and weiner roasts. 
Let nothing interfere with the magic 


Toronto , Canada , April 1959 


123 


of the peace pipe, the council fire and 
the Indian challenges. 

To be really effective, the Indian 
Council Ring needs splashes of colour. 
Br : ght red, blue, yellow, rust and black 
can be displayed in blankets, painted 
shields, tom toms, totems etc. Feathers 
pro difficult to locate except at Thanks¬ 
giving and Christmas when arrange¬ 
ments can be made with turkey raisers. 
Select the round ended wing feathers 
as they are best for headdresses. Scraps 
of coloured felt, pieces of fur, old fedora 
hats and cow horns from the local 
abattoir are also useful items to collect. 
A reasonably good tom tom may be 
made from a cheese box, and old drum 
heads are sometimes available from 
music stores. The chief requires a war 
bonnet and the medicine man should 
have a headdress made of horns, fur 
feathers and streamers. If feathers are 
plentiful, all staff and campers should 
wear one or more. Snipped fringes 
sewn to a pair of khaki slacks, and 
down the sleeves of a khaki shirt, worn 
with the tail out, makes an adequate 
and picturesque costume. As time goes 
on, it may be possible to acquire beaded 
buckskin shirts and moccasins. Addi¬ 
tional colour may be added by covering 
the lids from bushel hampers with can¬ 
vas or brown paper and painting 
Indian designs or totems on them. 

The frequency with which you hold 
council rings is up to you. If daylight 
saving prevails in your camp, it is 
difficult to wait until it is dark to start 
your programme. The Indian Council 
is more effective after dark but this is 
not essential. There is no excuse for 
the programme to drag. Just as in 
every activity, there is a limit beyond 
which interest lags, the best Indian 
Councils seldom last more than one 
hour. 

Let us assume then that the site is in 
readiness. The fire is built but not lit. 


The order of procedure is typed on a 
small card in case some details escape 
your memory; and the campers are all 
eager and curious about the big night. 

It is suggested that campers prepare 
for the Council at their own cabins 
under the guidance of their counsel¬ 
lors. While there, they should adjust 
headbands, apply war paint (a water 
colour paint) and prepare tribal yells. 
When the tom tom starts to beat, they 
leave their cabins and proceed in single 
file to the Council Ring. It is most 
effective when the camp proceeds in a 
quiet, orderly fashion, in complete 
silence from the time they enter the 
trail leading to the council ring until 
the ceremonies begin. The chief and 
his assistants may be seated at the 
council rock during this assembly period 
or if they wish, they may enter after 
everyone is seated. If the latter is done, 
the camp should stand when the chief 
and his entourage enter. 

Each Council Ring should have a 
definite pattern and include certain 
features, always keeping in mind that 
one hour is the time limit. The time to 
stop is when the campers want more. 

The following is suggested as a stan¬ 
dard outline: (1) Fire Lighting and 
Peace Pipe Ceremony — 5 minutes. 

(2) Indian Games — 15 minutes. 

(3) Pageant or stunt — 5 minutes. 

(4) Rangers Reports — 15 minutes. 

(5) Closing — Hiawatha’s Departure 
and Omaha Tribal Prayer—20 minutes. 

Indian Games are highly successful 
if a definite procedure for challeng¬ 
ing is instituted and maintained 
throughout. These games should be re¬ 
served for use at the Council Ring and 
each should be introduced by giving it 
an Indian origin. Even such characters

HOW RETARDED 
SCOUTS CAN 
ENJOY CAMP 

From — The Scout Leader 
Published by 

The Boy Scouts Association 



“Scouting is for all boys!” This is 
not just a slogan or a theory—it’s a 
fact. Across Canada at the end of 1957 
there was a total of 31 Scout Groups 
operating for handicapped boys, the 
blind, deaf, crippled and mentally re¬ 
tarded. Scouting for the handicapped 
increased by 20 per cent last year. The 
adaptability of the Scout programme 
is perhaps nowhere better demonstra¬ 
ted than when it is used for handi¬ 
capped boys. 

Let us take one example. Dr. Harold 
Frank, graduate of McGill, Queen’s 
and Toronto universities, a noted med¬ 
ical practioner and psychiatrist is the 
Superintendent of the Ontario Hospital 
for the Mentally Retarded at Smiths 
Falls. Himself a former Scout, Dr. 
Frank introduced Scouting into his in¬ 
stitution as both a recreation and a 
therapy several years ago. Its pheno¬ 
menal success at Smiths Falls has been 
carefully watched by similar institu¬ 
tions in other parts of the country. 
Today there are Scout Groups opera¬ 
ting in nine mental institutions in 
Canada. 

At Smiths Falls, Scouting is a twenty- 
four-hour-a-day activity. Even in the 
dormitories and the dining hall the boys 
are grouped in Patrols and Sixes, and 
this system is extended to their school 
work. 


Recently Canadian Headquarters’ 
representatives had the opportunity of 
seeing Scouting for the mentally handi¬ 
capped in action at a summer camp. 
At Ottawa’s “Opemikon” campsite, 
seventy-five miles from the capital, a 
full Troop of Scouts from the Smiths 
Falls institution held their annual sum¬ 
mer camp. Their camping standards — 
from our observations — would be 
assessed as much above average. 

The Scouts lived in Patrols, cooked 
their own meals, indulged in ordinary 
waterfront activities such as swimming 
and boating, washed their dishes, made 
gadgets, went hiking and generally 
followed the same kind of programme 
as would any other Troop. Some boys 
even did their first class journey during 
the camping period. 

They went further than that. They 
did a “Good Turn” for the camp—as 
they had done in the previous year. 
Their 1958 effort was to clear a large 
section of the waterfront of brush to 
make possible an early extension of the 
beach and swimming area for another 
one hundred yards. 

Later in the summer Wolf Cubs 
from the same institution also camped 
at Opemikon, as they had done in 1957. 
'These boys, under capable direction, 
do their everyday Scouting and their

SPRING 

VISTAS 

F. M. Van Wagner, President 
Canadian Camping Association 


Spring has returned and camping 
season is rapidly approaching. It is 
with some feelings of regret that we 
put our skiis away, for they have pro¬ 
vided us with a most enjoyable way to 
keep in touch with our favourite rural 
haunts during winter week-ends. There 
is much of interest to be seen along the 
ski trails, but when the sap begins to 
run, buds swell and burst, the snow- 
shoe rabbit and ermine change their 
white coats for brown. We too must 
adjust to the changing season. 

Camp Directors will look forward 
to the first visit to camp. A quick check 
to sec if any winter damage has oc¬ 
curred, then begins the extensive pro¬ 
gramme of improvements, repairs and 
possibly additions that must be com¬ 
pleted before the arrival of campers, 
still many weeks away. During these 
spring visits to camp, we will see and 
hear much activity, as all around us 
nature responds to the eternal call of 
spring. There is so much of interest at 
this season it is too bad our campers 
could not share it with us. 

There are many things we would 
like our campers to gain from their 
stay at camp. Every camp will have its 
special objectives and fields of major 
interest, influenced largely by the in¬ 
terests of the Directors. This I acknow¬ 
ledge to be true in our case. We are 
most desirous that above all else our 
campers will develop an interest in, 
and an appreciation for the things of 



nature and life in the out-of-doors. One 
of our society’s greatest needs at pres¬ 
ent, and perhaps even more in the 
future, is for outdoor recreation in all 
seasons. 

The ability to enjoy the out-of-doors 
and its many interests and attractions 
is not inherited, it must be acquired. 
At present few of our adult citizens arc 
making use of the extensive rural areas 
available across our country for their 
recreation. A programme of outdoor 
education is definitely needed. The 
realization of this fact is leading many 
schools in the* United States to provide 
limited camping for all pupils. Certain¬ 
ly the best time to gain the interest 
and skills essential to our enjoyment 
of simple outdoor life is during our 
younger days. Most boys and girls res¬ 
pond readily to such opportunities. 
Given proper guidance, they will 
quickly learn the fundamentals of good 
camping and an interest in nature that 
may result in their becoming life-long 
outdoor enthusiasts. Nowhere can such 
training be given as well as in our 
summer camps. 

How often are we told that camp 
programmes should be built around 
those activities closely related to our 
environment? What finer contribution 
can our camps make than to provide 
campers with experience that will en¬ 
able them in later life to return to our 
parks and forest areas, there to enjoy 
the beauty, peace and quiet so essential 
to their physical and mental well-being 
and so difficult to find elsewhere?

REPORT FROM MADRAS 

On Professor Charles E. Hendry’s recent 
trip to India, he visited Camp Tonakela for 
the opening ceremony and dedication of the 
Girls’ Convalescent Pavilion, in memory of 
the late Dr. Hedley S. Dimock. 


It was the Chief Minister’s first visit 
to Tonakela. 

He spoke, of course, in Tamil which 
is the language of the Madras area. I 
could not understand his words, but I 
understood perfectly the spirit of what 
he said and so did the score or more 
of English-speaking guests who with 
my wife and myself watched the eager 
faces of the guests from Madras city, 
and the several hundred campers and 
villagers from nearby who gathered in 
the large Council Ring to hear the 
Chief Minister of Madras State, the 
Honourable Sri. K. Kamaraj, open the 
Annual Day of “Friends of Camp 
Tonakela”. The occasion was the un¬ 
veiling of a tablet on the main pillar 
of a new convalescent girls’ unit at the 
camp, in memory of one of camping’s 
most respected leaders and one of camp 
Tonakcla’s staunchest friends, the late 
Dr. Hedley S. Dimock. 

Girl campers from Avvai Home, an 
orphanage; boys from the Rainbow 
Club Free Night School, Perambur; and 
two groups of campers from the Poon- 
amallee School for the Blind, put on 
a delightfully entertaining programme 
of Indian dances, pyramid building and 
music. In the background, just as I had 
remembered them before, in ever in¬ 
creasing numbers as they managed to 
leave their work in the paddy fields 
and walk the long distance involved, 
the villagers watched with unimagin¬ 
able eagerness and with the quiet 
dignity of peasants who belong unmis¬ 
takably to the soil upon which they 
stood. 

Before gathering in the large earthen 
Council Ring, the numerous adult 


guests were served tea and refreshments 
by gracious ladies in colorful saris, and 
the Chief Minister with attendants 
made the rounds of the camp. He 
stopped and talked individually with 
three boys in the convalescent unit, and 
with villagers; and he asked discerning 
questions, obviously intent upon getting 
a genuinely accurate understanding of 
the operation. He went into the dining 
hall, inspected the native type kitchens, 
stood by one of the deep 16 ft. diam¬ 
eter wells — the best in the area — 
paused to admire the swimming pool 
(a rarity indeed), and glanced inside 
one of the many tents being used by 
the campers. 

Along the way they found shade and 
fragrance from hundreds of trees which 
had been planted and tended with 
much care over the past twelve years. 
The grounds were spotless, the build¬ 
ings neat and clean, and everywhere 
hung garlands and decorations made 
from leaves and native materials which 
had been gathered and worked into 
attractive designs and put in place by 
twenty village youths who worked until 
2:30 o'clock in the morning to have 
everything in perfect readiness. 

Here where I sit writing this brief 
account of the big day, on the porch 
of Wallace Forgie’s cabin, there is an 
acacia tree whose delicate festive 
branches bow down to form a huge 
umbrella at least forty feet in diameter, 
providing a shaded outdoor seclusion 
and a kind of serenity one associates 
with the silence of a sanctuary. 

A short time ago we stood under 
other gracious trees to see forty little

Toronto, Canada, April 1959 


131 




continued from page 129 
children from the nearby villages 
get their special free breakfast. Each 
morning, like clockwork, they come for 
this very essential food. Seated on straw 
mats on the bare ground, they had just 
begun to sing their morning prayer of 
thankfulness, the solo part being sung 
by a bright young boy who seemed to 
be a key person. This prayer, too, was 
in Tamil. It was later translated for 
me: 

“The Holy Omnipresent! 

Grace us with your presence to bless us 
That do not forget Thee in prosperity 

or poverty. 

We praise Thee, we bow down to gain 

Thy benediction.” 

The record of service of this impres¬ 
sive demonstration camp and convales¬ 
cent centre parallels the magnificent 
quality of the physical plant and the 
beauty of the natural setting. Over the 
years some 30,000 boys and girls have 
camped on these grounds and the 
earlier site. Last year 6,000 visits for 
sterile dressings and other medical care 
were made by villagers to the daily free 
clinic of the Minor Treatment Centre. 
With the opening of the pavilion for 
girls, accommodation is now available 
for forty convalescents at a time. Some 
six hundred boys have already benefit- 
ted by this important and highly suc¬ 
cessful programme. Yesterday morning 
when I visited and spoke at the school 
for the Blind, the principal pointed out 
the first girl received in the convales¬ 
cent unit. She had suffered from Ty¬ 
phoid, and the school was helpless to 
provide the essential diet, but she is 
now fully recovered. Although blind, 
she is about ready to begin her univer¬ 
sity studies. 

In the camp as a kind of mascot (the 
minimum age is 8 years) is a little lad 
of five years whose mother died when 
he himself was in hospital. No one 
knows his family name, no relatives 
appeared, and he is completely alone 
in the world. First as a convalescent 


and now as a ‘permanent resident’ at 
Camp Tonakela, he had discovered that 
he is not alone. His given name is 
‘Jararaj’ and for his family name, used 
only as initial in India, he has ‘Tona- 
kcla’. He is a great favorite and his 
prospects are bright indeed. 

It is not surprising that the Chief 
Minister was most favorably impressed 
with Camp Tonakela. In his remarks 
he acknowledged with real apprecia¬ 
tion the contribution made by campers, 
camp leaders and friends in the United 
States and Canada. He complimented 
those in charge on the sound founda¬ 
tions underlying the administration of 
the camp. Having come in a jeep from 
the main road, and having seen the 
poor condition of the winding approach 
to the camp, he took the initiative in 
saying that he would see that proper 
access was made available. He also 
agreed to have a plaque made for the 
new unit of the enlarged Minor Treat¬ 
ment Centre which is to be called after 
him. 

Sri. W. R. Gopal Ratnam and his 
charming and talented wife presided 
over the Saturday celebrations. Mr. 
Ratnam is Chairman of the Camp 
Tonakela Committee, Madras. Other 
members of the Committee also par¬ 
ticipated actively. In the background 
one could discern the fine guiding hand 
of Wallace Forgic, and the efficient 
administration of N. Perumal Naidu, 
the Camp Director. Everyone shared 
in the day’s activities with moving 
pride. 

Greetings were received from the 
Overseas Fellowship of Campers and 
Friends of Camp Tonakela, and a 
letter of good wishes was read from 
‘Ted’ Cavins, representing both the 
North American Committee and the 
American Camping Association. Here 
at Camp Tonakela it became abun¬ 
dantly evident that World Brother¬ 
hood is a reality. The East and West 
are here engaged in friendly and fruit¬ 
ful collaboration. —©

continued from page 120 

In the light of this consideration, 
what then becomes of our concern for 
values ? Should we put our values aside 
and search for young people who will 
become accepted leaders of children? 
This doesn’t seem to me to be a satis¬ 
factory approach. We can all think of 
counsellors who could lead their camp¬ 
ers, but in directions we’d rather they 
did not go. Should we then search for 
counsellors who will lead campers in 
directions we want them to go? This 
is not quite a satisfactory approach 
either, I think, because this implies we 
are looking for nothing more than bell 
cows. It seems to me we are searching 
for individuals who fundamentally 
share our values but have ideas of their 
own too, and who also possess those 
characteristics which enable them to 
become leaders of children. 

Now I believe we’ve finally arrived 
at the point at which most seaches for 
leaders start: What are the character¬ 
istics of people which make them 
leaders? What are those mysterious 
qualities which place a few individuals 
above the mass of followers? The vol¬ 
uminous research on leadership has 
mainly aimed at the answer to this very 
question. The answer we get has be¬ 
come increasingly clear: there are none 
you can count on. This may be dis¬ 
appointing for those who have been 
looking for such help in their search 
for leaders. But scientific findings lead 
to this discouraging conclusion. Gibb, 
in his summary of leadership research 
writes . . studies of the personalities 
of leaders have failed to find any con¬ 
sistent pattern of traits which charac¬ 
terize leaders.” And Professors Cart¬ 
wright and Zander, in their standard 
text, Group Dynamics, conclude, u On 
the whole, the attempt to discover the 
traits that distinguish leaders from 
nonleaders has been disappointing.” 


The pressure of evidence has forced 
social psychologists to give up the 
Great Man theory of leadership. We 
have begun to look elsewhere besides 
to the individual for the factors which 
generate leadership. It has proved fruit¬ 
ful to think in terms of critical combin¬ 
ations of personal characteristics with 
the demands of the leadership situation. 
The right characteristics in the right 
time and right place add up to leader¬ 
ship. A simple example: we would not 
expect the leader of a den of thieves to 
be elected chairman of, say, a minister¬ 
ial conference. Some fruitful results 
have developed from research which 
began this situational theory of leader¬ 
ship. 

Some research of my own, for ex¬ 
ample, shows that elementary school 
classmates who represent the values the 
children hold are more apt to become 
peer group leaders. But different groups 
of children have different values and 
would choose different leaders. For the 
seven-year old girls in the study, it was 
important that a leader not fight very 
much; but seven-year old boys could 
accept a fighter as their leader. And it 
was important to twelve-year old boys 
and girls that boy leaders be good at 
games, but girls didn’t have to be. 

We also have some research findings 
on what adolescent boys and girls ex¬ 
pect of adult leaders. Here too, the 
requirements of boys and girls differ. 
Over 2,000 boys and 2,000 girls in a 
nationwide sample were asked what a 
scoutmaster or a girl scout leader 
should be like. Greatest agreement 
among the boys was that a leader 
should have technical skills, know how 
to do things; 40% gave that answer. 
But only 25% of the girls thought this 
was a necessary characteristic of lead¬ 
ers; 76% of the girls thought that 
personal characteristics of affection, 
consideration, and such were more im- 


Toronto, Canada, April 1959 


135 



portant. Only 34% of the boys men¬ 
tioned these things in their image of 
leaders. 

But among adolescent boys taken by 
themselves there are differences in 
leader ideals. For example, most four¬ 
teen-year old boys expect a leader to 
organize and initiate activities. But 
most sixteen-year olds reject this kind 
of leader, looking for one who will be 
available to help them when they need 
help, but otherwise letting them run 
their own show. It is clear that one 
leader image will not do for all leader¬ 
ship situations. 

So our search for leaders becomes 
very complicated indeed. It seems we 
have two alternatives: either we hire 
counsellors to go with particular groups 
of children, or we hire people with 
unlimited potentialities, so they can fit 
any situation they encounter. The 
second alternative is appalling; we 
despair of finding many of that breed. 
But the first is not so bad. In fact, it 
has certain attractive features. 

Picking counsellors to go with certain 
groups of campers means that, facing 
an applicant for a job, we do not ask, 
“Is he the type I want?” but rather, 
“Where in my camp would this fellow 
fit?” We break out of our stereotyped 
image of the leader and think in terms 
of types of leaders for different jobs 
around camp. Suddenly we find many 
more applicants are potentially good 
counsellors. I’m convinced that, with 
this orientation, about 80% of the 
people who apply for camping jobs are 
good risks. The fellow who seemed a 
little shy, and admitted he wasn’t much 
of an athlete, might, on our impression 
of his sensitivity to people, become an 
excellent counsellor for our little boys. 
The young lady who wasn’t very 
“campy” but skilled in modern dance 
and quite attractive in a sophisticated 


sort of way might be perfect for our 
senior girls. 

In order to apply this “situational 
selection” approach to hiring success¬ 
fully, we should know what kinds of 
leaders our campers will accept. In 
part, our experience tells us which 
counsellors are likely to be appropriate 
with which children. But how many of 
us have thought actually to ask the 
campers themselves? It might be 
illuminating, and fun too, to hold bull 
sessions with campers on “What kind 
of counsellors would you like to have?” 
If we do this without threatening their 
present counsellor’s feelings of ade¬ 
quacy, he too can learn something 
about being a better leader. Campers 
of all ages can respond to the question, 
I’m sure. 

But further, it seems to me that the 
problem of our search for leaders has 
a third alternative solution, one which 
is apt to be the most profitable. Grant¬ 
ing that our search is for people who 
will fit into particular situations and 
become leaders, and assuming that 
about 80% of applicants could be used, 
we certainly cannot expect that many 
will be perfect fits. That is, we must 
think in terms of hiring raw material, 
whom we teach on the job to be 
leaders. This is probably my most im¬ 
portant point. Wc must be prepared to 
train. 

Training is, after all, the real pay-off 
and the constructive element of super¬ 
vision. Not patrolling camp to see if 
counsellors are at the waterfront, and 
not pounding at rules and regulations 
at individual and group carpet sessions. 
Good supervision helps a counsellor do 
the best job he’s capable of, by helping 
him use his unfolding experiences to 
improve his performance. We help him 
tailor himself for the job he faces. We 
help him acquire the skills he needs; 
we help him develop the sensitivity to 


136 


Canadian Camping 



campers he needs; we help him maxi¬ 
mize the potential he has for earning 
a leadership position. 

Research on the qualities of success¬ 
ful scoutmasters demonstrates that the 
best of them consider their primary 
function to be training, training assis¬ 
tant scoutmasters, and training patrol 
leaders to carry on with their boys. 
Leaders with this orientation did not 
find large troops a burden. Rather they 
wanted more scouts and more assistants 
to whom they could give the benefit 
of their experience. 

Well, then, if our search is for raw 
material we can train, how do we 
know good raw material when we see 
it? I’ve spoken already about some of 
the characteristics of good raw material 
when I sketched the leader image to 
which my camping values lead; he 
fundamentally shares my values; he’s 
widely curious; and he’s sensitive to 
others’ interests and feelings. I think 
I can add to this description of good 
raw material now. If we look ahead to 
training people, we should be looking 
for people who have a good chance of 
learning. This means, first, that an 
applicant is motivated to do a good 
job with children; he wants to be a 
good counsellor. Second, he doesn’t 
think he knows it all; it is a positive 
sign for us if he is a little unsure about 
whether he will be a good counsellor. 
If an applicant is under the impression 
he will have everything under control, 

I suspect he will not be very open to 
learning experiences. 

How do we get information to evalu¬ 
ate an applicant as raw material? Un¬ 
fortunately, our sources of information 
are scarce indeed, which should set us 
to thinking seriously about how to get 
maximum use out of them. Essentially, 
we have just two ways to get to know 
an applicant: through recommenda¬ 
tions of others and through a personal 


interview. You’ll note, I do not count 
the application blank he fills out as a 
source of information. My feeling is 
that this form is useful only as a basis 
for interviewing. 

The personal interview can be a 
wonderful source of information if we 
use it skillfully. But I fear a lot of us 
use an interview to sell our camps to 
applicants and learn little about them 
except their ability to nod apprecia¬ 
tively. How do we discover an appli¬ 
cant during an interview? 

Well, first, I think we ask him to fill 
out an application blank, before he 
gets a chance to learn, by talking with 
us, what kind of answers we want. The 
application asks him for: 1) a descrip¬ 
tion of himself, in terms of age, height, 
weight, health, and so forth; 2) his 
current occupational status, as a stu¬ 
dent or what, and where; 3) all his 
occupational history, not only his 
camping or related jobs; 4) other rele¬ 
vant, non-occupational experiences, in¬ 
cluding experience as a camper; 5) an 
inventory of his skills (the familiar 
check list which often indicates degree 
of skills); 6) and an inventory of his 
interests, in terms of hobbies, extracur¬ 
ricular activities at school, and so forth. 
Specialized camps might want to in¬ 
clude certain other questions, but I 
think these I’ve mentioned are basic. 

After we look over the application 
for a few minutes to get some notion 
of what the applicant is like, we begin 
an interview. And I think, with all the 
information we may already have, it 
is still wise to begin with a request 
like, “Well, tell me something about 
yourself.” We start completely open 
like that to let the interviewer tell us 
what he thinks is important about him¬ 
self. This gives us some insight into 
what his values are. If a fellow starts 
by reeling off the important fraternity 
and campus positions he holds, I learn 


Tor onto, Canada , April 1959 


137 



that he’s a “Big Wheel” and he wants 
me to know it. If he starts with the 
large salaries he’s made over the past 
few years, I am warned in advance 
about the major issues involved in my 
hiring him. If he starts with his feelings 
about how camp experience fits in with 
the career he’s set his sights on, I learn 
something about his perspective on jobs 
I may have open and where he might 
fit best. 

The most important thing about be¬ 
ginning an interview, though, is that 
the interviewer is listening and the 
applicant is talking, and talking about 
himself. No description of camp is 
given at this point, no pictures of the 
sailboat fleet on the lake tantalize him. 
The director and his camp arc still 
unknown for the applicant. 

Next comes a question less open than 
the first, but still open: “What have 
you got to offer boys and girls at camp? 
What do you think you can do for 
them?” Again we get at the applicant’s 
values: We might learn if he is skill- 
oriented or personality-oriented; we 
might get a better picture of which of 
his skills he values; we might learn 
what he thinks camping is all about. 
After approaches like these, I think we 
begin probing about specific items on 
the application blank. Age, for ex¬ 
ample: “May I see some proofs of your 
age?” This becomes more than an age 
test; it is a character test as well. 

We might go down the list of camps 
the applicant has worked at and asked 
simply, “Why aren’t you going back?” 

We might test his knowledge of ac¬ 
tivities he says he can lead, by asking 
him “How often have you been horse¬ 
back riding this last year?” ... “Which 
saddle do you prefer?” and so forth. 

We might test his degree of interest 
in something, by probing, “What photo¬ 
graphic equipment do you presently 
own?” 


In such ways as these wc test the 
strength and depth of the information 
on the application form. While it is 
essential for the applicant to know 
about our camp, we save that for later. 
When we begin to tell him about our¬ 
selves, we may again use the interview 
situation to probe for the interviewee’s 
values and his notions about camping. 
For we begin with a remark like, “Well, 
I know something about you now. I 
think you should know about our camp. 
Why don’t wc begin with your ques¬ 
tions. What do you want to know?” 

What does the applicant ask? 

“How much do you pay counsellors?” 

“Are there girls (or boys) at camp 
too, or at least nearby?” 

“What kind of children come to 
your camp?” 

“Do you have a camp theater?” 

What do his questions tell us about 
him? 

Before the interview is over we 
should make certain that the applicant 
knows enough about us to make an 
intelligent decision. He should know 
what our camp is like, what our values 
are, what his job might be, what our 
personnel practices are, how our salary 
scale runs, etc. When he’s satisfied and 
we’re satisfied, the interview is over. 

We could spend hours on the ap¬ 
praisal interview alone. I’ve tried to 
indicate what I think a valuable one 
is like. Let’s go on now to discuss 
recommendations for a few moments. 
For the most part, I’m afraid they con¬ 
sist of broad generalities hinting at 
vague personal qualities. Often they 
come from people who are really in no 
position to evaluate the applicant’s 
potentialities as a camp counsellor. We 
can take steps to improve the letters of 
recommendation we get, first by telling 
the applicant specifically whom we

continued from page 138 

want letters from, and second, by spe¬ 
cifying the kind of information we 
want. 

During the course of the appraisal 
interview, we discover the applicant’s 
previous camping or other job experi¬ 
ence. I suggest we pick those which 
seem, for their relevance, the best 
sources or evaluations and ask for 
letters from these employers. If the 
applicant thinks others are more ap¬ 
propriate for some reason, he may 
supplement our list, but not substitute. 

We’re wise to provide sources of in¬ 
formation with standard forms. We get 
more, better, and comparable informa¬ 
tion that way. We should tell our 
sources what kind of job the applicant 
is being considered for to help them 
get some context for their evaluations. 
Then we should ask for a clear de¬ 
scription of the job or role the appli¬ 
cant filled for them: was he a junior 
counsellor, a waterfront specialist, a 
student in a lecture course of 300? This 
helps us place evaluations in context. 
The standard form then asks questions 
which get at dimensions of counsellor 
material important to us, as determined 
by our leader images. 

It seems to me camp directors owe it 
to each other to be as honest and 
complete as possible in exchanging 
letters of recommendation. Sometimes 
it’s hard to remember a counsellor, 
especially if he was on the staff more 
than a year ago. We can improve our 
exchange of information if we keep a 
file of counsellor evaluations. These 
evaluations should resemble the stan¬ 
dard forms requesting information 
which I’ve mentioned, covering the 
same dimenisons. They should be filled 
out by the counsellor’s immediate camp 
supervisor and checked by his director. 


140 


Canadian Camping 





Now, we should have no compunc¬ 
tion about sharing these evaluations 
with our colleagues. They represent, 
after all, the most valuable source of 
information we have on counsellor po¬ 
tential. It seems to me these evaluations 
serve another important function, too. 
They are important to the training we 
do. An evaluation form should be 
familiar to a counsellor from the be¬ 
ginning of camp, perhaps from the 
appraisal interview itself. It sets the 
goals for which a counsellor shoots; it 
makes clear the aim of in-service train¬ 
ing; it exposes the criteria by which he 
will be re-hired or not. 

This evaluation should be a shared 
thing. The counsellor should discuss it 
while it is being filled out. He should 
have the opportunity to comment upon 
it, adding to it if he wishes. Ideally, an 
evaluation should not be filed unless it 
bears the counsellor’s signature, testify¬ 
ing that, with his additions if necessary, 
the evaluation reflects the job he did. 
If we are to share evaluations with 
other camp directors, a counsellor’s 
knowledge of it and chance to rectify 
it is an ethical must. Further, we can 
then feel more comfortable sharing it 
with other campmen. And we must not 
overlook its importance as a training 
tool, central to the process of super¬ 
vision. 


But I can’t go into training and 
supervision at this point. This is a 
whole other aspect of camp organiza¬ 
tion for which we haven’t time now. 
This is the place for summarizing. 

I’ve suggested that we take certain 
steps in our search for leaders. First, 
we should get a clear image of our 
object. His image grows out of our 
self-conscious concern with our own 
values, which help shape the image. We 
must also find out from our campers 
what they want in leadership, for their 
values also shape the leader image. 

Second, we must recognize that there 
are, within the limits of our values, 
many leader types, so we should con¬ 
sider applicants with all our pro¬ 
gramme and campers in mind, trying 
to fit different people into different 
spots. 

Third, we must maximize the infor¬ 
mation we gather about an applicant 
by working to improve our letters of 
recommendation and our personal in¬ 
terview techniques. 

And fourth, we must expect to dis¬ 
cover mainly raw materials rather than 
polished counsellors. We must train. 
We must put at least as much effort 
as we put in the search for leaders into 
the creation of leaders.

By G. C. Toner 


THE MONARCH BUTTERFLY 

Recently, the Brodie Club of the 
Royal Ontario Museum at Toronto, had 
as its guest speaker Dr. Fred A. Urqu- 
hart, Director of the Division of Zoology 
and Palaeontology of the Royal On¬ 
tario Museum. His subject was the 
migrations of the Monarch butterfly. 
Dr. Urquhart has had many years of 
experience with these insects, and the 
Brodie Club lecture was a brief summary 
of the natural history of one of our 
most familiar butterflies. 

The life history of the Monarch starts 
when the female lays a single egg on 
the leaf of a small milkweed. Several 
hundred eggs may be laid by each 
female but only a single egg is deposited 
on each leaf by the same female though 
others may lay their eggs on the same 
leaf. When the caterpillar hatches in 
several days it is very small, hardly 
thicker than a pin and only a fraction 
of an inch in length. Its first meal is 
usually the eggshell from which it 
hatched. 

The larva grows quickly on its diet 
of milkweed leaves, shedding its skin 
as it outgrows it, until at the end of a 
week or so it is as long and stout as a 
man’s little finger. It is dressed in a 
green skin with bars of black and white 
and occassional spots of gold, familiar 


Canadian Camping 



to many people as the “milkweed worm”. 
As it reaches the end of the larval period 
it must find a place where it will be 
undisturbed throughout the next stage, 
its life as a pupa. 

The pupal stage is the transformation 
of the larva into the adult butterfly. 
Metamorphosis, the name given to the 
change, means that every’ organ, even 
the form of the larva, changes to con¬ 
form with the shape of the adult insect. 
As well, sufficient fat must be stored in 
the adult body to last it through its life, 
body to last it through its life. 

The fat storage of the Monarch is 
considerable for it must last till the 
migration is completed. The fat only 
needs water, as supplied by the nectar 
sipped from flowers to supply the adult 
with energy to fly immense distances on 
its migrations. 

The migration of this butterfly may 
be unique among insects. Dr. Urquhart 
has served as the focal point of many 
co-operators who are engaged in stud\ r - 
ing the movements of the creature. 
Briefly, the migration is as follows. Part 
of it is only conjecture but so much is 
known that the unknown may be 
guessed by the informed ones. 

In early September the adult butter¬ 
flies gather together and in small groups 
and singly set out for the south. Large 
bodies of water arc skirted; at Toronto 
the movement is west and south to get 
around Lake Ontario, and the insects 
move at a fair pace towards their goal. 
When the temperature drops at night 
the butterflies cling to the branches and 
the leaves of certain trees that seem to 
be suitable for roosting and overnight 
stay. 

Day after day the insects travel south. 
Thunderstorms, winds that force them

out over large lakes and cold fronts that 
kill millions of the migrants, all take 
their toll. But the survivors, and they 
are many, for untold millions started 
the trek, disappear into Mexico. In the 
spring they return though no proof of 
this has been discovered. 

Dr. Urquhart marks the butterflies 
with a paper label glued to the wing. 
Both label and the glue used are spe¬ 
cially prepared, very light and very 
tough. The marking party must be 
afield early to catch the insects when 
they are still numb from the early 
morning chill. The tree where the 
butterflies are resting is shaken and they 
fall into a prepared net. The net is 
emptied into a large carton and in this 
they are transported to a screened porch. 
Here, they can be tagged at leisure. 

Returns have not been plentiful. 
Butterflies are not scanned like birds 
and many of the returns have been 
made by children whose sharp eyes 
have noted the tag. Spring returns are 
particularly scanty but Dr. Urquhart 
hopes in time to build a knowledge of 
the migration throughout the year. 

MARTEN 

The decision of Lands and Forests 
to transfer live marten seems to me 
to be very wise. The more breeding 
colonies that are established the better 
will be the chances of survival. Marten 
are found in the Bancroft area to a 
very limited extent. Every year or two 
one will be caught and they have all 
been taken in the wild country to¬ 
wards Algonquin Park and northwest 
of Bancroft. 

Live marten, or sable lured into 
traps with strawberry and raspberry 
jam and fish, have just been trans¬ 
ferred from Algonquin Park to a new 
home in the Lindsay district in the 


eastern part of the Province — a first 
for that area. Live-trapping has been 
used for some years by the Ontario 
Department of Lands and Forests to 
expand beaver population in deficient 
areas. 

Live-trapping marten calls for im¬ 
agination and ingenuity, Fish and 
Wildlife Division officals explain. 
Traps, collapsible for easy carrying, 
are set along waterways 75 to 100 feet 
from the water’s edge in dense, dark 
and mixed heavy timber. Fish is hung 
just behind the trap pan; jam is placed 
on the pan. Jam and cod liver oil also 
can be used. The cod liver oil draws 
the marten to the trap and the jam 
entices him in, a spring closing a door 
behind him. Traps are covered with 
sticks and brush and made to resemble 
a hollow log. 

Traps must be inspected daily be¬ 
cause marten are high strung, nervous 
animals and if left more than one night 
in the trap are usually found dead in 
the morning. Special holding pens are 
used to keep them in captivity until 
transfer and release in new homes. In 
the interim, dog food is substituted for 
their natural food. 

“To assess the success of marten re¬ 
stocking and transplanting, each ani¬ 
mal released has a numbered metal tag 
inserted in one ear and a 1 number tat¬ 
tooed on the o t h e r,” conservation 
officers say. 

It is hoped that the transplanted 
marten will form the nucleus for even¬ 
tual successful trapping of this valuable 
little fur-bearer in the Lindsay area. 
The restocking programme is to be 
continuous over the next few years, 
Lands and Forests officials say. 

Marten, or sable, is an abnormal 
weasel about two-thirds the size of a 


144 


Canadian Camping 


house cat, with soft, lustruos pelage, 
broad rounded ears, long lithe body, 
short legs provided with sharp claws, 
and a noticeably bushy tail. Coloura¬ 
tion generally is yellowish brown, rich¬ 
er and dark above the thrpat. The 
chest is conspicuously lighter, being 
orange or ochracious buff. There is a 
marked seasonal difference in colour. 
The summer pelage is darker, thin and 
harsh, but becomes soft and heavier in 
winter. 

The little animals originally were 
distributed all over Ontario. But, 
through relentless trapping, they have 
disappeared from most of their former 
range. Algonquin Park and the Chap- 
leau Crown Game Preserve are, in 
fact, two of their last main strongholds. 

Principal foods during the summer 
are mice, squirrels, chipmunks and 
berries. The habits of marten are little 
known, due largely to the habitat it 
occupies. In recent years, however, the 
Department’s Research Division has 
produced much information on the 
species. It retreats before the advance 
of civilization, yet is of an inquisitive 
and curious nature, thus falls easy prey 
to traps. It is agile and equally at 
home in the trees or on the ground. 

Mating occurs in late July or Aug¬ 
ust, but development is arrested for 
several months. The three to five young 
are born in late April or early May 
after a gestation period of 31 to 33 
weeks. At birth the young are blind, 
helpless and covered with fine yellowish 
hairs. The eyes do not open until the 
youngsters are nearly six weeks old. 
Adult weight is attained in about three 
months when the females weigh ap¬ 
proximately 1.6 pounds and the males 
2.5. 

The nest is made in some rotten 
snap, hollow trees or den. Due to its 
small size, the marten is able to utilize 


the holes made by the big pileated 
woodpecker. 

In such retreats, a nest of leaves is 
prepared and here the marten spends 
the greater part of the day in sleep, 
emerging at night to hunt. It is often 
active also in the day, however. Its 
colour and general physiognomy sug¬ 
gests a small fox, particularly so when 
the marten is seen on the ground. 

The species is easily trapped, even 
during periods of heavy snow. The fine 
quality of its fur and the price it com¬ 
mands have caused a great reduction 
in its numbers. Lumber operations 
also have dealt it a severe blow, be¬ 
cause much of the territory which was 
formerly occupied by marten has now 
been destroyed. Marten prefer a mixed 
forest of mature timber with balsam 
and a sprinkling of cedar, with a gen¬ 
erally good dense canopy of conifers 
and hardwoods as habitat. 

TRANSPLANTING SEEDLINGS 

Although the transplanting of natural 
tree seedlings for ornamental purposes 
should be attempted only in the spring 
and fall, specifically May or October, 
this is the time of year when we have 
time to plan, time to read and learn 
instructions, to gather our How-To 
material, and save pitfalls during the 
busy season. 

Unfortunately, foresters of the Lands 
and Forests Departments tell us, many 
tranpslanted seedlings never grow, many 
brought in from the country are never 
planted, they just sit and die. These 
experts have jotted down a few tips for 
camp gardeners and trees-men. Perhaps 
success will be yours if you can profit 
by experience, and the camp grounds 
can take on new beauty with new trees. 

A spade or shovel should be used to 
dig . . . never pull . . . the seedling; 
take as much soil as possible with the 
roots. 

continued next page 


Toronto , Canada , April 1959 


145 



It is generally true that the smaller 
the tree, the better the chance of success 
in transplanting. 

Pack the lump of soil tightly into a 
container to keep the earth from rattling 
off the roots and to cut down evapora¬ 
tion of moisture. 

Plant the seedling in its permanent 
location as soon as possible. 

The lump of soil adhering to the 
roots should be firmly pressed into the 
planting hole with the heel to exclude 
air pockets. 

Water the trees frequently until they 
are well established. 

It is inevitable that the root system of 
the larger transplants will be disturbed 
and its ability to absorb moisture and 
nutrients decreased proportionately. To 
compensate for the reduced root effi¬ 
ciency it is advisable to reduce the leaf 
area, as much as 50%. The wide 
branches could be shortened or, if this 
will spoil the form of the tree, break 


off some of the buds along the twigs. 
The main stem of the tree should be left 
intact to preserve the inherent beauty 
of the species. 

By following these steps, experts say, 
the precentage of transplanted trees that 
grows will be greatly increased and the 
necessity for repeated planting will be 
''liminated. 

Evergreens are frequently used as low 
ornamentals on lawns or for planting 
to hide building foundations. Deciduous 
trees serve best for shade and to pro¬ 
vide background for the building site. 
Of these, basswood, soft maple, elm and 
white birch are the most common. 

Lands and Forests officers warn pros¬ 
pective planters: “Before you remove 
trees from any property, you should 
obtain permission from the owner. 
Though it will be many years before 
they have monetary value as timber, 
these small seedlings have a real value 
as an immature crop.” —•

THEORY OF 
SEPTIC TANK 
OPERATION 

John E. Dean 


Increased emphasis on sanitation and 
health in the summer camp make it 
essential that owners and directors have 
a better working knowledge of sewage 
disposal. It is hoped that the following 
information will be of help in this 
respect. 

As the greatest problems lie in the 
operation of septic tanks, we will con¬ 
centrate on them. The septic tank is 
nothing more or less than a receptacle 
into which sewage can be ejected and 
left for a certain length of time in 
order that a bacterial agent may break 
the sewage down to some degree. It 
should be free of sun-light and oxygen. 
Septic tanks are generally designed to 
provide a working capacity for a 
known number of persons. Thus, their 
size can vary greatly, depending on the 
job they will be expected to do and the 
number of persons who will be ex¬ 
pected to use them. 

It is advisable to contact the local 
health unit when contemplating the in¬ 
stallation or modification of sanitary 
systems or sewage disposal systems. The 
health unit will provide you, not only 
with the latest information and by¬ 
laws, but will inspect the work to en¬ 
sure that it has been done properly. 

One of the greatest misconceptions 
involving the operation of septic tanks 
is the belief that septic tanks complete-

in

and

camp medical supplies is FREE on 
request.

The Latest 16 mm Motion
