Toronto, Canada, April 1959 


147 




ly do away with all solid matter. This 
can be disproved quite easily. Assume 
that all matter, both liquid and solid, 
which flows into the tank is immediate¬ 
ly subjected to a burning process. No 
one will dispute that an ash will remain 
as the end product. How then can it be 
expected that a less efficient process, 
such as an anearobic bacterial process, 
will completely eliminate all solids? 
The residue left from the bacteria will 
be many times gerater than that left 
from the burning process. 

Another factor involved is that sep¬ 
tic tanks are no longer used merely as 
septic tanks. They were originally de¬ 
signed merely for the disposal of sew¬ 
age. These days many foreign materials 
must be permitted entry into the septic 
tank as a matter of modern day con¬ 
venience and sanitation. The bacteria 
upon which the septic tank depends for 
its efficiency will not attack many of 
these materials, so that they remain 
almost entirely as solids. In the same 
vein, chemicals are known to retard, 
if not prevent the bacteria from grow¬ 
ing. This of course would mean that 
the sewage waste itself would remain 
almost in its original state. Such are 
some of the abuses affecting the effici¬ 
ent operation of a septic tank. Let us 
now see what actually happens from 
the scientific point of view. 

As we have said, bacteria are respon¬ 
sible for the chemical and physical 
changes which occur inside a septic 
tank. The anearobic bacteria actually 
attack and digest sewage, producing a 
minute but nevertheless solid residue. 
This residue is certainly less than or¬ 
iginal bulk of the material but is never¬ 
theless a residue and remains as such 
everafter, building up on the bottom 
of the tank. This residue is called 
sludge. 


Another process concurrent with the 
production of sludge is the creation of 
a scum. When the bacteria have lived 
their short life span out, they float to 
the surface where, together with greas¬ 
es, soaps and other buoyant materials, 
they form a scum. This scum may be 
many feet in thickness in certain in¬ 
stances and with the consistency of 
loam. As with any bacterial action, 
heat is produced which will in most in¬ 
stances prevent the septic tank from 
freezing in moderately cold weather. 

During the process of putrefaction 
(breaking down of sewage by the bac¬ 
teria) a very powerful and dangerous 
gas is produced called methane. Me¬ 
thane is easily ignited and can asphyxi¬ 
ate persons subjected to it. Generally, 
septic tanks are vented, either with a 
breather attached to the septic tank 
or by means of a vent stack installed 
through the roof of the building to 
carry away offensive odors. 

The scum and sludge accumulations 
eventually reach a point where one of 
two things may occur. Firstly, the scum 
may become so heavy that it may 
either impede or stop the flow of waste 
products from discharging into the sep¬ 
tic tank. The drain subsequently fills 
with liquids causing the lowest fixture 
to over-flow. The second, more costly 
and least noticed problem which might 
arise is that the sludge may over-flow 
into the tile-bed, eventually sealing it 
off. This may result in either the 
plumbing backing up or water seeping 
up through the ground over the tile or 
septic tank area. 

These two above problems can be 
easily remedied by systematic cleaning 
of the septic tank. A competent septic 
tank company can gauge the proper 
pumping period required in any in¬ 
stance to protect campers from incon¬ 
venience. This operation should be 
done either in the Fall or late Spring. 


148 


Canadian Camping 



Periodic cleaning contracts or emer¬ 
gency service may be obtained from 
most conscientious firms in this business. 

Most people who utilize septic tanks 
have probably asked “what can I put 
into my septic tank to help it along?” 
It was suggested above that the bac¬ 
teria responsible for the action are 
believed to emanate from the body. 
Thus, in a new tank or one that has 
just been cleaned, the action will begin 
automatically, provided the liquid me¬ 
dium in the septic tank is one which 
will stimulate bacterial growth. This 
growth will be retarded by a liquid 
medium consisting of too great an al¬ 
kaline content. Soaps, greases, etc. may 
cause this condition to arise and should 
be avoided in over-abundance (as 
should the over-indulgence of acids). 
Generally speaking, the greater the al¬ 
kaline content of the tank, the less the 
bacterial action. To over-come this al¬ 
kalinity, the addition of commercial 
septic tank conditioners is advisable. 
Caution should be observed when using 
these chemicals, as they will burn skin, 
clothes and other materials. 

Many people prescribe the use of 
yeast, but from all available reports, 
particularly those from the United 
States, yeast does not make the septic 
tank operate any more efficiently. It 
should be remembered that if the tank 
is in an alkaline state no amount of 
artificial starters, however great, will 
aid digestion — it must be neutralized 
and brought back to a slightly acidic 
state. 

If there are any problems or ques¬ 
tions which we have not had time to 
discuss in this brief article, please send 
them to The Editor, Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Magazine, or the author, and an 
answer will be forthcoming in later 
editions of Canadian Camping.

A recent letter from our kind friend, 
Mr. John P. Kidd, Executive Director 
of the Canadian Citizenship Council, 
Ottawa, brought the following com¬ 
ment and suggestion: 

“In browsing through the February 
issue of Canadian Camping — this is 
a wonderful little magazine and it 
seems to be getting more interesting 
with every issue—the thought occured 
to me that a number of the camps 
would have both as staff and as camp¬ 
ers a number of recently or relatively 
recently arrived immigrants. 


Toronto , Canada , April 1959 


151 



I don’t know whether I have sent 
you a copy of New Roots in Canadian 
Soil, but in any case I am enclosing 
one. It is an attempt to explain the 
complex processes of adjustment of 
immigrants to Canadians; it might just 
be of some help to camp leaders.” 

An excellent publication such as this 
goes into great detail about the back¬ 
ground, the work, the social adjust¬ 
ments, the potentials, the status of 
these people who are joining us by the 
thousands. It can surely help us as we 
help them.

ship Council, 180 Bay Street, Ottawa, 
Ontario. (50^) 

WORSHIP WAYS FOR CAMP 

Clarice Bowman 

When our objectives as camp staff 
move from the tangible to the intang¬ 
ibles and reach Spiritual Values, we all 
are a little uncomfortable. There is so 
much that we would like to do; the 
problem of how to do it effectively is 
ever with us. Clarice Bowman in 
Worship Ways for Camp has attempt¬ 
ed to deal with part of this problem, 
and so she deserves a special “Thank 
You”. Her book should be on every 
camp bookshelf, for she offers both 
method and material which would be 
useful for all camps. 

The book begins with a section on 
Worship, and then it branches into 
two separate divisions: Young Campers, 
and Juniors and Young Teens. In very 
readable language full of stimulating 
ideas (your counsellors would find it 
very helpful), she explains the needs 
and interests of these two groups, and 
how it affects their “worship”. Then 
she also includes two very suitable an¬ 
thologies of materials. The selections 
are up-to-date, closely connected with 
camp life and experiences, in meaning¬ 
ful language for the age groups, and 
include prayers, poems, and short, 
short stories. 


Certain camps would wish to supple¬ 
ment this with their own church ma¬ 
terials, but I doubt that many anthol¬ 
ogies would be so carefully prepared 
or so usable. G. R. Welch & Co., 
Toronto. $3. 

SERVICES FOR THE OPEN 
Mattoon and Bragdon 
Services for the Open is an old 
standby.... I couldn’t do without it. 
It is more formal, more traditional in 
its selection of materials, but it con¬ 
tains such a variety of truly beautiful 
poetry, meditations and prayers suit¬ 
able for special days, every day, all 
kinds of weather and all kinds of ex¬ 
periences related to camp. It always 
provides more than enough for all oc¬ 
casions. It does not include any theory, 
but does contain suitable hymns with 
music. G. R. Welch & Co., Toronto.

M Govan 

WORTH IT ALL 

My face is burned, 

My skin has peeled, 

My hair is bleached and dry. 

My legs are bruised, 

My arms are scratched, 

My breath comes with a sigh. 

My weight’s gone up, 

My appetite 
Is sharper than a knife. 

I’ll have to start 
To take off pounds 
When back to normal life. 

But when I think 
Of morning watch 
And evening vesper song, 

Of chattering girls 
In happy games, 

My aches and pains are gone. 

To help one girl 
Draw’ nearer God, 

And start the upward trail, 

Brings me reward 
For all the work 
That days at camp entail. 

Edna F. Grant, 

20 Gerrard St. East, Toronto, Ont .

as Pat and Mike become Indian braves 
scouting in the woods, each intent on 
scalping the other. Enthusiasm runs 
high during the Indian games and 
campers and staff alike will let off 
steam. The games should never drag. 
The best time to stop them and go on 
with the rest of the programme is when 
interest is high. 

The pageant or stunt should be 
prepared in advance by some cabin 
group. Such things as Indian dances; 
Indian stories or plays; blood brothers; 
weaving rush mats; naming the tribes; 
visiting an Indian Burial Ground etc., 
are suitable for this part of the pro¬ 
gramme. The chief introduces the event 
and everyone sits back to watch. 

Ranger Reporting is an audience 
activity just like the Indian Games. 
The chief sets the stage by commenting 


on the redman’s ability to observe de¬ 
tail. A standard procedure can be 
taught whereby the campers relate in¬ 
teresting things they have observed 
around the camp or on the trail. Often 
a story concerning birds can be turned 
into a fascinating period on nature lore; 
especially if the chief is quick to seize 
the opportunity to question the narra¬ 
tor regarding details of size, habitat, 
plumage and so on. The fifteen minutes 
assigned to this section slips quickly by. 

By now, the fire has burned low 
and night is upon us. We have partici¬ 
pated in games as Indians; we have 
indicated our prowess as orators and 
now is the time for the chief to bring 
the council to a successful close and 
leave that lasting impression. Hiawa¬ 
tha, that wise and brave chief of long 
ago is at the end of his journey. His 
faithful chieftains mourn his departure

as he moves off into the blackness of 
night with a song on his lips. Once he 
has gone and the mourners depart, the 
chief wants to know if there are any 
braves ready to take his place. Several 
young whelps respond and fail the test 
of walking on fire. Finally, one young¬ 
ster succeeds and qualifies to step into 
the shoes of the departed Hiawatha. 
The chief warns him that the first test 
is an easy one; now he must take his 
hunting knife and depart to live alone 
in the woods. When night comes he 
may build a small fire for his all night 
vigil. During the dark night, he will be 
frightened many times by the unknown. 
Wild eyes will surround his small 
campfire and he will be tempted to 
grab his hunting knife to disperse the 
intruders. That is when he must refrain 
and prove that he has the Great Spirit. 
That is when he must stand alone and 
sing the song which we shall teach him. 
Here the chief leads in the singing of 
the Omaha Tribal Prayer. 


The young man leaves the silent 
Council Ring and presently a small fire 
is seen at the top of the cliff. A young 
Indian brave stands, and with his hands 
stretched overhead he sings the Indian 
words which mean, “Father a Needy 
One Stands Before Thee, I Who Pray 
am He”. The chief says quietly “Know 
we that our Council is ended”. The 
ring quietly empties as the camp retires 
in single file to bed. 

The Indian Council Ring can be 
developed slowly and surely over the 
years. Convincing leadership is the key 
and only after conducting a number of 
ceremonies will you begin to develop 
confidence and feel the emotional ap¬ 
peal of the redman. 

From “Indian Council Ring” 
by W. ]. Eastaugh,

A LOW-COST SWIMMING POOL 

In 1947 Perth Presbytery acquired 
property and built an inland camp for 
boys and girls up to fifteen years of 
age. There arc fifteen acres of woods, 
hills and excellent flats for a playing 
field. 

In 1948 they built a swimming pool 
25 x 60 feet, six feet deep for 20 feet 
and sloping up to 2/2 feet in the re¬ 
maining forty feet. The walls are ten 
inches thick and the floor is five inches 
deep. There is very little steel in the 
walls and none in the floor. In 1950 a 
filter was made. It is much like a small 
farm cistern and is filled with gravel 
and sand. Water from the pool is 
pumped through the filter and back 
into the pool at the rate of about 
fifty gallons per minute. The pump is 
driven by a three-quarter H.P. motor 
and runs night and day while camps 
are in progress. 

The pool is emptied, cleaned and 
refilled before camp opens. During 
camping, water is added to replace 
what is lost in back-washing the filter. 
At the end of camping the pool is left 
full, and it remains filled until the end 
of June. This keeps the winter frost 
out of the walls and floor. The pool has 
been through eight winters without 
frost damage and this has kept the cost 
of construction within the narrow limits 
of a camping budget. 

The filter has kept the water clean 
so that the water meets the health re¬ 
quirements and adds immeasurably to 
the safety of the campers. Any child in 
trouble can be seen without difficulty. 

The pool, sidewalks, filter and pump¬ 
ing equipment cost approximately 
$1,600.00. 

Detailed information about the pool 
and filter, with drawings, can be pro¬ 
cured from the camping committee. 
Transparencies can be procured from 
A. H. Johnston, 14 Balaclava Street, 
St. Thomas, Ontario.

PAPIER-MACHE 

Tear up several sheets of newspapers 
into small pieces like snow-flakes. Place 
in a large bowl. Add enough water to 
saturate paper. Knead paper with 
hands as if kneading dough. After 
paper is thoroughly kneaded and still 
damp, add flour. Continuing kneading 
until pulp is entirely mixed and pasty. 

To make paste — 1 cup flour, 4 cups 
cold water (oil of cloves, few drops, to 
keep paste longer) mix flour and water 
well, let stand until flour is dissolved 
about 20 minutes. Cook mixture over 
low heat until transparent, stirring 
constantly. Remove from fire and place 
in a covered jar. 

LEAF SMOKE PRINTING 

Materials: leaves, white typewriter 
paper, candle, pure lard or shortening. 

Rub sheet of typewriter paper with 
small amount of pure lard. Use just 
enough lard to make the paper look 
transparent. Hold greased side of paper 
over a candle flame until paper is 
smoked black with a heavy velvet-like 
appearance. Place leaf, vein-side down, 
on the smoked surface. Cover with a 
clean sheet of paper. Rub carefully 
with fingertips. Make certain entire 
leaf is covered with the black smudge 
smoke. Remove leaf. Place it, vein-side 
down, on clean sheet of paper cover 
with another sheet of paper. Rub with 
fingertips to transfer leaf pattern on 
sheet for final print. These prints are 
permanent and will completely show 
the delicate texture and vein formation 
of the leaves. 

Final suggestion: Use powdered 
Tempra Paints for economy sake.
